extraction.name: Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research
extraction.description: We present the Natural Questions corpus, a question answering data set. Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results,and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; and a further 7,842 examples with 5-way annotated sequestered as test data. We present experiments validating quality of the data. We also describe analysis of 25-way annotations on 302 examples, giving insights into human variability on the annotation task. We intr oduce robust metrics for the purposes of evaluating question answering systems; demonstrate highhuman upper bounds on these metrics; and establish baseline results using competitive methods drawn from related literature.
extraction.creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov
extraction.citeAs: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 7, pp. 453–466, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present. The annotation process involves presenting an annotator with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair, and the annotator returns a (long answer, short answer) pair. Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface, by a pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds. The task is divided into three conceptual stages: Question Identification, Long Answer Identification, and Short Answer Identification.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Web API
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Both the long and short answer can be NULL if no viable candidates exist on the Wikipedia page. Annotators can disagree about whether or not a document contains an answer to a question (i.e., whether or not L=NULL). In cases where annotators agree that an answer is present, they can still disagree about the correct assignment to the answer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. The evidence documents are Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results for these queries.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Simple heuristics are used to filter questions from the query stream. The goal of these heuristics is to discard a large proportion of queries that are non-questions, while retaining the majority of queries of 8 words or more in length that are questions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are filtered using simple heuristics. Questions are run through the Google search engine, and only those where a Wikipedia page is in the top 5 search results are kept. Part of speech tags and entities are identified using Google’s Cloud NLP API, and Hearst patterns are used to find a broad set of hypernyms for categorical noun phrases.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Comprehensive guidelines were developed for the task. The annotation process involves three stages completed by a single annotator: 1) Question Identification: Contributors determine if a question is good (fact-seeking, answerable with entity/explanation) or bad (ambiguous, incomprehensible, false presuppositions, opinion-seeking, not factual). 2) Long Answer Identification: For good questions, annotators select the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, whole list) containing enough information to infer the answer, or mark 'no answer'. 3) Short Answer Identification: For examples with long answers, annotators select the entity/entities within the long answer that answer the question, or flag 'yes', 'no', or 'no short answer possible'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Analysis of 25-way annotations on 302 examples provides insights into human variability on the annotation task. Post-hoc evaluation of annotation quality was performed, with long/short answers having 90%/84% precision, respectively. Four experts, who prepared the guidelines, independently annotated examples for correctness and then met to discuss disagreements and reach a single consensus judgment. The analysis showed that for naturally occurring questions, there is often genuine ambiguity and multiple acceptable answers, leading to disagreement among annotators regarding the presence and location of answers.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; 7,842 examples with 5-way annotated for test data; and 302 examples with 25-way annotations for variability analysis.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Queries are anonymized and aggregated. No other sensitive human attributes are explicitly mentioned as collected.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Open-domain question answering (QA) is a benchmark task in natural language understanding (NLU) with significant utility to users. The dataset is intended to drive the development of methods for NLU.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The choice of Wikipedia as the source of factual information may introduce biases, as with any dataset.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on longer queries (8 words or more), potentially limiting its scope. Future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia. There is often genuine ambiguity and variability in acceptable answers, and short answers can be arbitrarily delimited, leading to extreme variation. Models may struggle with list-formatted data.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed to provide large-scale end-to-end training data for the QA problem, to drive research in natural language understanding, and to serve as a new benchmark for research in QA. It is suitable for Training, Testing, and Validation of question answering systems.
